root_cause: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (clot in brain drainage vein), from estrogen pill plus dehydration

patient.name: Maya Lindqvist
patient.background: Biology student, started combined contraceptive pill 6 weeks ago; mother had 'leg clot'.

findings.result: Left drainage vein blocked, no flow: sinus thrombosis
Swollen optic discs from high skull pressure: papilledema
Clot breakdown marker very high: elevated D-dimer
Inherited clotting tendency gene present: Factor V Leiden
Mild lining irritation from ibuprofen: gastritis
Concentrated urine, mild dehydration: raised urea
Clear lungs, no clots: normal perfusion
Deep veins compress normally, no DVT
Spinal fluid clear, no infection: normal CSF
Slightly raised enzymes from alcohol: mild transaminitis

treatments.name: Heparin (blood thinner) + fluids
treatments.why: Anticoagulation stops the venous clot growing and lets the sinus reopen, even if small bleeds exist; stop the pill.
treatments.attending_line: A blood thinner for a headache. Congratulations, you read the venogram.

treatments.name: Sumatriptan (migraine drug)
treatments.why: Triptans constrict blood vessels, worsening flow in an already congested brain and promoting venous infarction.
treatments.attending_line: Migraine in a 21-year-old with a weak hand. Bold. Wrong, but bold.

treatments.name: Dexamethasone (steroid)
treatments.why: Steroids don't help sinus thrombosis and increase clotting risk, plus raise blood sugar.
treatments.attending_line: Steroids: when you don't know what it is, make it worse anti-inflammatorily.

treatments.name: Morphine + anti-nausea drip
treatments.why: Masks pain while the clot grows; opioid sedation raises CO2, widening brain vessels and skull pressure.
treatments.attending_line: She's comfortable now. So is anyone in a coma.

post_mortem: Estrogen from her new pill, an inherited Factor V Leiden mutation, and hangover dehydration caused a clot in a brain drainage vein, raising skull pressure. The clues were a headache worse lying down, a new pill, a family clotting history, and a weak hand, which together point away from migraine.

root_cause: Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus) with enlarged spleen

patient.name: Jordan Okafor
patient.background: First-year student, rugby player, new girlfriend; no medical history, no allergies.

initial_symptoms.text: Severe sore throat, white tonsil patches

findings.result: Many large odd white cells: atypical lymphocytes
Monospot test positive: heterophile antibodies
Liver enzymes mildly raised: viral hepatitis pattern
Spleen enlarged under left ribs: splenomegaly
Tonsils swollen with white exudate: tonsillitis
Rapid strep test negative: no Streptococcus
Fast but regular heartbeat: sinus tachycardia from fever
Lungs clear, no pneumonia: normal auscultation
Urine slightly concentrated: mild dehydration
No neck stiffness, alert: meningitis unlikely

treatments.name: Rest, fluids, no contact sports
treatments.why: EBV is viral so antibiotics do nothing; supportive care plus avoiding sport for weeks protects the swollen, fragile spleen.
treatments.attending_line: Boring, correct, and nobody gets an itchy rash. I hate how right you are.

treatments.name: Amoxicillin (antibiotic)
treatments.why: Antibiotics don't kill viruses, and amoxicillin in mono triggers a widespread rash in most patients.

if_wrong_cascade.text: Itchy red rash covering whole body
Watery diarrhea from gut flora disruption

treatments.attending_line: Congratulations, you treated a virus with penicillin. He's now polka-dotted.

treatments.name: IV ceftriaxone, admit
treatments.why: Broad-spectrum antibiotics miss the virus and wipe out gut bacteria, letting C. difficile take over.
treatments.attending_line: Bigger gun, same imaginary bacteria. The C. diff thanks you.

treatments.name: Ibuprofen, clear for rugby
treatments.why: A tackle can rupture the enlarged spleen, and NSAIDs impair platelets, worsening the internal bleeding.
treatments.attending_line: Great, send the walking water balloon into a scrum. What could go wrong?

post_mortem: Jordan caught Epstein-Barr virus through saliva, and it looked exactly like strep throat, but the negative strep test, atypical lymphocytes and enlarged spleen showed it was mono. A good doctor would have noticed the shared water bottle, two weeks of exhaustion and the left-side ache at rugby, and kept him off antibiotics and off the pitch.

patient.name: Maya Okafor
patient.background: First-year student, new dorm, skipped campus meningitis vaccine. Otherwise healthy.

initial_symptoms.text: Deep aching leg pain, cold feet

findings.result: Cloudy spinal fluid, many white cells: bacterial meningitis
Bean-shaped paired bacteria: gram-negative diplococci
Purple spots don't fade when pressed: petechiae
Platelets dropping, clotting factors used up: early DIC
Mild swelling of brain linings: meningeal inflammation
Bones and muscle normal; pain from poor perfusion
Mild lining irritation from alcohol: gastritis
Clear lungs, fast breathing: tachypnea
Slightly reduced filtering: early acute kidney injury
No fluid or swelling: normal joints

treatments.name: IV ceftriaxone, immediately
treatments.why: A third-generation cephalosporin crosses inflamed meninges and quickly kills Neisseria; hours matter.
treatments.attending_line: Look at that, the antibiotic for the bacteria. Revolutionary.

treatments.name: Acyclovir (antiviral)
treatments.why: Treats herpes encephalitis but does nothing to bacteria, so sepsis keeps progressing.
treatments.attending_line: Great, you've cured a virus she doesn't have.

treatments.name: Heparin for leg clot
treatments.why: Leg pain is sepsis-related poor perfusion, not a DVT; anticoagulating someone in DIC with low platelets triggers bleeding.
treatments.attending_line: She's already bleeding into her skin. Let's help it along.

treatments.name: Fluids and antiemetic only
treatments.why: Treating nausea as gastroenteritis delays antibiotics while bacteria multiply in blood and meninges.
treatments.attending_line: Hangover protocol for a girl with a rash. Bold.

post_mortem: Maya picked up Neisseria meningitidis from her roommate's vape and the crowded dorm, and it spread from her throat into her blood and meninges. The leg pain and cold feet came first and pointed away from the brain, but light sensitivity plus non-blanching spots in an unvaccinated student meant ceftriaxone right away.
